title: 20 tests of nothing. Any hits?
hook: Each test has only a 5% chance of a false alarm. So twenty tests are safe. Are they?

knows: that a result can be called 'significant' at a 5% false-alarm rate
doesNotKnow: how false-alarm chances compound over many tests

misconception: If each test has a 5% false-alarm rate, a batch of 20 tests also has only about a 5% chance of producing a false alarm.
objective: The learner can explain that the chance of at least one false alarm grows with the number of tests (1 - 0.95^20, about 64% for 20 independent null tests), so a single 'finding' among many tests is weak evidence.

claims.text: For 20 independent tests of true nulls, each with a 5% false-alarm rate, the chance of at least one false alarm is about 64%.
The chance that all 20 stay quiet is 0.95 multiplied by itself 20 times, about 36%.
On average, a batch of 20 such tests produces one false alarm.
The stage's batches are seeded independent tests with a 5% false-alarm chance each; the first 1,000 bulk batches give 638 with at least one alarm (63.8%).
claims.source: src/demos/probability/twenty-harmless-tests/model.ts, seed 4 (picked from seeds 1-8 for a first batch with 2 alarms; seeds 1-8 gave 61.8%-66.8% over 1,000 batches). Batches 1000-1999: 638 with an alarm, 996 alarms in total; batches 2000-2999: 636.

claims.text: The 64% figure assumes the tests are independent and that none of the 20 has a real effect.
claims.source: Assumption stated in the lesson. With dependent tests the chance differs (for positively correlated tests it is usually lower).

recall.question: A study checks 40 foods against a disease, each at a 5% false-alarm rate, and reports one 'significant' food. How impressed should you be?
options: Very: only a 5% chance it is a fluke
Not much: with 40 tests, about 2 false alarms are expected
It proves the other 39 foods are safe
recall.why: 40 x 5% = 2 expected false alarms even if no food matters, and the chance of at least one is 1 - 0.95^40, about 87%.
